newsitem.title: UK: EMU woes to inspire US, gilts, Bunds.
newsitem.headline: EMU woes to inspire US, gilts, Bunds.

text.p: As worries over prospects for a single European currency continue to simmer, international bond investors are increasing their exposure to bonds previously immune to EMU euphoria, analysts said on Monday.
Concerns were stoked after a survey by Der Spiegel magazine said 77 percent of Germans want economic and monetary union (EMU) delayed from its planned start date of 1999.
"We're advising switching out of Spain into the U.S., and out of Italy into the U.K.," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London.
"Any delay to EMU would be viewed as a derailment," she said.
She said the trades were most attractive in the five-year area of the curve, and were particularly good value if they were both hedged to cover the currency risk.
Analysts said convergence trades, the darling of the bond markets in 1996, had slowed to a virtual standstill, with investors worried they may go into reverse as 1997 progresses.
Reed said the spread between 10-year Italian BTPs and comparable German Bunds would widen back towards the 200 basis point level by the end of the year. It was at 164 basis points by 1400 GMT.
She said the Bonos/Bund spread would widen to 175 by year-end, compared with a current level of 118 basis points.
That view of so-called deconvergence trades in European bonds was supported by a survey of 38 fund managers conducted by Lehman Brothers.
The survey of fund managers, who invest $140 billion, showed that only 26 percent were overweight Italian bonds in February, compared with 39 percent in January.
David Brown, chief international economist at Bear Stearns in London, said a likely beneficiary of position-switching would be German Bunds and other core European markets.
"It's going to go back into hardcore Europe, it's going to go back into Bunds and it's going to go back into the Netherlands," he said.
He said German yields would continue to head lower from a fundamental perspective, but would also head lower on the back of deconvergence flows.
Don Smith, international economist at HSBC Markets, said there was evidence that the recent lira sell-off had prompted investors to do an about turn on Italy and take profits.
He said gilts' "safe-haven" status from the machinations of EMU was probably worth around 20 basis points of outperformance for the gilt/Bund spread.
The gilt/Bund spread is currently at 175 basis points, and Smith saw that narrowing to 140 basis points by mid-year and 120 points by the year end.
"So long as a Labour government fulfills expectations of being as conservative as the Conservatives, gilts will outperform whether EMU goes ahead or not," said Smith.

The ruling Conservative government must call an election within the next three months. The opposition Labour Party, who have not held power since 1979, are currently almost 20 percentage points ahead in opinion polls.
Even if there were signs that EMU was a brighter prospect, analysts said the bulk of the convergence is already over -- offering little but the dregs for potential investors.
"There's so much overconfidence already built into the whole convergence in Europe," said Brown.
"And if you look at the risk bias ahead, it is much more skewed towards big deconvergence rather than the last residues of convergence."
